source: Contradicting evidence for both cis and trans-phosphorylation mechanisms has, for example, been reported for AurA (Dodson et al., 2013; Zorba et al., 2014), the checkpoint kinase, Chk2 (Cai et al., 2009; Dodson et al., 2013; Oliver et al., 2006), IRAK4 (Cheng et al., 2007; Ferrao et al., 2014), the insulin receptor (IR) kinase (Frattali et al., 1992; Shoelson et al., 1991; Wu et al., 2008; Yamada et al., 1992), and PKR (Dey et al., 2014; Dey et al., 2005; Mayo et al., 2019), among others.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dey et al., 2014, Dey et al., 2005, and Mayo et al., 2019.

claim: Models of cis-autophosphorylation have been proposed for GSK3β.
source: Models of cis-autophosphorylation have been proposed for GSK3ß (Cole et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cole et al., 2004.

claim: Models of cis-autophosphorylation have been proposed for DYRKs.
source: Models of cis-autophosphorylation have been proposed for GSK3ß (Cole et al., 2004), DYRKs (Lochhead et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lochhead et al., 2005.

claim: Models of cis-autophosphorylation have been proposed for PKD.
source: Models of cis-autophosphorylation have been proposed for GSK3ß (Cole et al., 2004), DYRKs (Lochhead et al., 2005), and more recently, PKD (Cobbaut et al., 2018; Reinhardt et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cobbaut et al., 2018 and Reinhardt et al., 2023.

claim: PKD is autoinhibited in trans and activated by cis-autophosphorylation.
source: PKD is autoinhibited in trans and activated by cis-autophosphorylation (Figure 3D; Reinhardt et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reinhardt et al., 2023 and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: It has been argued that kinases lacking an HRD motif in their catalytic loop (non-HRD kinases) are not activated by activation loop phosphorylation.
source: It has previously been argued that kinases lacking an HRD motif in their catalytic loop (so-called non-HRD kinases) are not activated by activation loop phosphorylation (Johnson et al., 1996; Nolen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johnson et al., 1996 and Nolen et al., 2004.

claim: The biochemical characterization of PKD, a non-HRD kinase containing an HCD motif, shows its activation by phosphorylation.
source: Nevertheless, the biochemical characterization of PKD, a non-HRD kinase instead containing an HCD motif, shows its activation by phosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the context of the previous sentence citing Reinhardt et al., 2023.

claim: Molecular modeling and mutagenesis in PKD demonstrated that the missing arginine in the HCD motif is replaced by a different arginine residue in the activation loop.
source: Molecular modeling and mutagenesis in PKD further demonstrated that the missing arginine in the HCD motif is replaced by a different arginine residue in the activation loop, whereby the side chain reaches into exactly the same position as the canonical arginine in HRD kinases (Reinhardt et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reinhardt et al., 2023.

claim: Mass spectrometry unambiguously demonstrates that PKD autophosphorylation occurs exclusively in cis.
source: Although the mechanism of autophosphorylation remains to be determined for PKD, mass spectrometry unambiguously demonstrates that the reaction occurs exclusively in cis (Reinhardt et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reinhardt et al., 2023.

claim: Protein kinase R (PKR), inositol requiring enzyme 1 (IRE1), PKR-like ER kinase (PERK), and NimA-related protein kinase 7 (NEK7) require back-to-back dimerization to induce their activation by autophosphorylation.
source: Finally, kinase domain dimerization may also lead to allosteric autoactivation. Protein kinase R (PKR), inositol requiring enzyme 1 (IRE1), PKR-like ER kinase (PERK), and NimA-related protein kinase 7 (NEK7), require back-to-back dimerization to induce their activation by autophosphorylation (Cui et al., 2011; Dar et al., 2005; Dey et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2008; Richards et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2011, Dar et al., 2005, Dey et al., 2005, Lee et al., 2008, and Richards et al., 2009.

claim: Whether PKR, IRE1, PERK, and NEK7 can accomplish the autophosphorylation of their activation loops in cis or require higher-order oligomerization is still the subject of debate.
source: Whether these kinases can accomplish the autophosphorylation of their activation loops in cis or require higher-order oligomerization is, however, still the subject of debate (Belyy et al., 2022; Korennykh et al., 2009; Mayo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Belyy et al., 2022, Korennykh et al., 2009, and Mayo et al., 2019.

claim: B-Raf activation depends on the formation of a back-to-back dimer.
source: As discussed earlier in the context of autoinhibition, B-Raf activation depends on the formation of a back-to-back dimer (Figure 3E; Park et al., 2019; Rajakulendran et al., 2009; Wan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Park et al., 2019, Rajakulendran et al., 2009, and Wan et al., 2004, and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Raf dimer is critical for the activity of B-Raf against its substrate kinase MEK.
source: The Raf dimer is critical for the activity of B-Raf against its substrate kinase MEK, which forms a heterodimer with the kinase domain of B-Raf that is homologous to the PDK1 homodimer (Levina et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Levina et al., 2022.

claim: MEK forms a heterodimer with the kinase domain of B-Raf that is homologous to the PDK1 homodimer.
source: The Raf dimer is critical for the activity of B-Raf against its substrate kinase MEK, which forms a heterodimer with the kinase domain of B-Raf that is homologous to the PDK1 homodimer (Levina et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Levina et al., 2022.

claim: Mutagenesis of the αG helix-mediated dimerization interface impairs both PDK1 and MEK activation.
source: Although the precise mechanisms of PDK1 trans-autophosphorylation (Figure 3C) and trans-phosphorylation of MEK by Raf (Figure 3F) are still not clear, mutagenesis of the αG helix-mediated dimerization interface impairs both PDK1 and MEK activation (Haling et al., 2014; Levina et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haling et al., 2014 and Levina et al., 2022.

claim: Kinases of the IKK family, including IKKε and TBK1, form constitutive dimers in which the kinase domains are arranged in a back-to-back configuration by a helical stalk domain and a ubiquitin-like domain.
source: Finally, kinases of the Inhibitor of kappa B kinase (IKK) family, including IKKε and TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) form constitutive dimers in which the kinase domains are arranged in a back-to-back configuration by a helical stalk domain and a ubiquitin-like domain (Larabi et al., 2013; Tu et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Larabi et al., 2013, Tu et al., 2013, and Xu et al., 2011.

claim: Activation loop autophosphorylation in IKKε and TBK1 has been proposed to be achieved by higher-order oligomerization in an analogous manner to the UPR kinases IRE1 and PERK.
source: Activation loop autophosphorylation has been proposed to be achieved in an analogous manner to the unfolded protein response (UPR) kinases IRE1 and PERK by higher-order oligomerization (Zhang et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2019 and Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: Intact mass spectrometry is precise to less than 1 Da in mass ranges up to 100 kDa and sometimes even up to 200 kDa.
source: Modern, well-calibrated instruments are precise to less than 1 Da in mass ranges up to 100 kDa and sometimes even up to 200 kDa (Donnelly et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Donnelly et al., 2019.

claim: Intact mass spectrometry is an essential quality control step that provides confidence in the interpretation of biochemical results.
source: In a more general sense, intact mass spectrometry is an essential quality control step that provides confidence in the interpretation of biochemical results (Elsner et al., 2019; Levina et al., 2022; Pokorny et al., 2021; Reinhardt et al., 2023; Truebestein et al., 2023; Truebestein et al., 2021; Truebestein et al., 2015; von Raußendorf et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Native mass spectrometry can capture non-covalent protein adducts such as ligand-bound species.
source: When performed under non-denaturing conditions, native mass spectrometry can capture non-covalent protein adducts such as ligand-bound species (Bennett et al., 2022; Byrne et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bennett et al., 2022, Byrne et al., 2016, and Smith et al., 2017.

claim: Native mass spectrometry can capture protein-lipid interactions.
source: When performed under non-denaturing conditions, native mass spectrometry can capture non-covalent protein adducts such as ligand-bound species (Bennett et al., 2022; Byrne et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2017), protein-lipid interactions (Agasid and Robinson, 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Agasid and Robinson, 2021.

claim: Native mass spectrometry can capture protein complexes.
source: When performed under non-denaturing conditions, native mass spectrometry can capture non-covalent protein adducts such as ligand-bound species (Bennett et al., 2022; Byrne et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2017), protein-lipid interactions (Agasid and Robinson, 2021), and even protein complexes (Mehmood et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mehmood et al., 2015.

claim: Phosphorylation can hinder proteolytic cleavage in tandem mass spectrometry experiments.
source: In addition, phosphorylation can hinder proteolytic cleavage, leading to erroneous conclusions regarding the degree of modification.
evidence: This is a statement about a technical limitation of the method based on established knowledge.

claim: Antibodies raised against a phospho-peptide may only recognize a specific subpopulation of the phosphorylated protein when multiple phosphorylation sites overlap the binding epitope.
source: In the case of multiple phosphorylation sites that overlap the binding epitope of the antibody, these antibodies may only recognize a specific subpopulation of the phosphorylated protein.
evidence: This is a statement about a technical limitation based on established knowledge of antibody specificity.

claim: Antibodies raised against multiply-phosphorylated peptides may fail to recognize proteins singly phosphorylated on the canonical phospho-site.
source: Conversely, antibodies that have been raised against multiply-phosphorylated peptides may fail to recognize proteins singly phosphorylated on the canonical phospho-site (Waldron et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Waldron et al., 2001.

claim: Western blotting is, at best, semi-quantitative, and at worst, non-specific.
source: Western blotting is, at best, semi-quantitative, and at worst, non-specific.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the technique based on established knowledge.

claim: Many antibodies are not specific and are contributing to a reproducibility crisis in molecular biology.
source: Finally, care must be taken in the validation of antibodies, many of which are not specific and are contributing to a reproducibility crisis in molecular biology (Frohner et al., 2020; Pillai-Kastoori et al., 2020; Schüchner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frohner et al., 2020, Pillai-Kastoori et al., 2020, and Schüchner et al., 2020.

claim: The autophosphorylation of five sites in FGFR1 was monitored using radionucleotide assays and the dynamics of each phosphorylation state was discriminated by time-resolved intact mass spectrometry.
source: An example of the successful combination of complementary techniques is the characterization of FGFR1 autophosphorylation (Lew et al., 2009). The authors monitored the autophosphorylation of five sites using radionucleotide assays and then discriminated the dynamics of each phosphorylation state in the population by time-resolved intact mass spectrometry.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lew et al., 2009.

claim: A concentration-dependent increase in kinase activity is usually interpreted as a bi-molecular reaction in trans.
source: The observation of a concentration-dependent increase in kinase activity is usually interpreted as a bi-molecular reaction in trans (Figure 4C).
evidence: This describes a common interpretation in the field, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Concentration-dependent kinase activity cannot distinguish between autophosphorylation in trans (face-to-face), autophosphorylation in cis (back-to-back), or trans-autophosphorylation via the face-to-face interaction of back-to-back dimers.
source: However, this cannot distinguish between autophosphorylation in trans (face-to-face), autophosphorylation in cis (back-to-back), or even trans-autophosphorylation via the face-to-face interaction of back-to-back dimers, as has been proposed for the UPR kinase IRE1 (Korennykh and Walter, 2012; Korennykh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Korennykh and Walter, 2012 and Korennykh et al., 2009.

claim: A dimerization-dependent decrease in kinase activity is indicative of autoinhibition in trans.
source: A dimerization-dependent decrease in activity is indicative of autoinhibition in trans (Reinhardt et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reinhardt et al., 2023.

claim: Autophosphorylation reactions that are not influenced by dimerization are not subject to any regulation in trans and likely proceed in cis.
source: Autophosphorylation reactions that are not influenced by dimerization are not subject to any regulation in trans and, as such, likely proceed in cis (GSK).
evidence: This is an inference based on the logic of the experimental approach.

claim: The gold standard way to discriminate between cis- and trans-autophosphorylation is to test whether an active kinase can phosphorylate an inactive copy of the same kinase.
source: The gold standard way to discriminate between cis- and trans-autophosphorylation is to test whether an active kinase can phosphorylate an inactive copy of the same kinase (Figure 4D).
evidence: This describes a standard experimental approach shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The autophosphorylation motif of some kinases is highly similar to the consensus substrate recognition motif and likely prone to trans-autophosphorylation at high concentrations.
source: An important consideration in the design of such experiments is that the autophosphorylation motif of some kinases is highly similar to the consensus substrate recognition motif and likely prone to trans-autophosphorylation at high concentrations, irrespective of whether this is the physiological mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference about experimental design considerations.

claim: In a unimolecular cis-autophosphorylation reaction, the enzyme converts itself into a product and the reaction can happen only once per molecule.
source: The simplest case is a unimolecular reaction, in which the activation loop is autophosphorylated in cis. If an enzyme converts itself into a product the enzyme is also the substrate and the reaction can happen only once per molecule.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the kinetics of a unimolecular reaction.

claim: Unimolecular cis-autophosphorylation is independent of concentration, diffusion, or substrate depletion, and proceeds with a constant catalytic rate until all enzyme has been converted into product.
source: It is, therefore, independent of concentration, diffusion, or substrate depletion, and proceeds with a constant catalytic rate until all enzyme has been converted into a product. This results in a linear increase of product over time until the reaction stops and the product remains constant (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the kinetics shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Trans-autophosphorylation is necessarily a bimolecular reaction in which the enzyme converts the substrate into a product.
source: The second case is autophosphorylation in trans, which is necessarily a bimolecular reaction in which the enzyme converts the substrate into a product.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the nature of trans-autophosphorylation.

claim: Trans-autophosphorylation is dependent on the association of the enzyme and the substrate, the intrinsic catalytic rate of the enzyme, and the dissociation of the product.
source: This reaction is dependent on (a) the association of the enzyme and the substrate, which is dictated by their interaction affinities and their respective concentrations, (b) on the intrinsic catalytic rate of the enzyme, and (c) on the dissociation of the product.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the factors affecting trans-autophosphorylation kinetics.

claim: In symmetric cis-autophosphorylation dependent on allosteric activation by back-to-back dimerization, the collision of two unphosphorylated molecules results in the phosphorylation of both.
source: A cis-autophosphorylation reaction that is dependent on allosteric activation by back-to-back dimerization is a bi-molecular reaction, therefore, concentration-dependent, even if the enzyme and the substrate are the same molecules. We designate the reaction symmetric if the collision of two unphosphorylated molecules results in the phosphorylation of both.
evidence: This is a definition and logical inference about a specific reaction mechanism.

claim: In symmetric trans-autophosphorylation, only homo-dimeric collisions are productive and the reaction rate decays with substrate depletion over time.
source: The autophosphorylation of an activation loop in trans requires the formation of a face-to-face dimer in which the phosphorylation site sits within the dimerization interface. Upon phosphorylation, the activation loop is stabilized in the active conformation and is no longer able to engage in such an interaction. This implies that only homo-dimeric collisions are productive and that the reaction rate decays with substrate depletion over time (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the kinetics shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In asymmetric trans-autophosphorylation, one kinase acts as an enzyme and one as a substrate, with productive interactions limited by stochastic conformational sampling.
source: In an asymmetric trans-autophosphorylation reaction, one kinase acts as an enzyme and one as a substrate. In the absence of phosphorylation to begin with, a productive interaction is only possible if one molecule adopts the active conformation while the second presents its activation loop as a substrate. This would presumably occur by stochastic conformational sampling, the efficiency of which limits the reaction by reducing the frequency of productive collisions.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the mechanism of asymmetric trans-autophosphorylation.

claim: Asymmetric trans-autophosphorylation results in sigmoidal kinetics.
source: Once phosphorylated, the kinase will be stabilized in the active conformation with a consequent gain in catalytic efficiency, which increases the reaction rate until the substrate becomes limiting. This behavior results in sigmoidal kinetics (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the kinetics shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Transient kinase domain dimerization must be associated with a means of locally concentrating reaction partners to overcome the dependence on diffusion for rapid signal transduction.
source: In the context of physiological signal transduction, transient kinase domain dimerization must be associated with a means of locally concentrating reaction partners to overcome the dependence on diffusion which would otherwise be incompatible with rapid signal transduction.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for physiological signaling.

claim: In the context of a constitutively dimeric kinase, bi-molecular cis- and trans-autophosphorylation are reduced to uni-molecular reactions with linear kinetics.
source: A conceptually interesting scenario is the constitutive dimerization of a kinase domain via a dimerization domain. The dimer can then be regarded as a single molecule, since the two kinases are at near-infinite local concentration, such that their autophosphorylation becomes independent of both concentration and diffusion. Bi-molecular cis- and trans-autophosphorylation are thereby reduced to uni-molecular reactions with linear kinetics that are only limited by the intrinsic catalytic rate (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the kinetics shown in Figures 5E-F.

claim: Kinetic data alone cannot necessarily discriminate between cis- and trans-autophosphorylation.
source: In summary, kinetic data alone cannot necessarily discriminate between cis- and trans-autophosphorylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of different kinetic scenarios.

claim: Dimerization of protein kinases must necessarily be transient and the free energy of binding must be low.
source: Dimerization of protein kinases, whether for the purposes of autoinhibition or autoactivation, must necessarily be transient and, therefore, the free energy of binding must be low.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the thermodynamic requirements for kinase regulation.

claim: If the kinase dimer interface is too strong, the kinase will be constitutively trapped in an inhibited or active state.
source: If the dimer interface is too strong, the kinase will be constitutively trapped in an inhibited or active state, respectively.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of strong dimerization.

claim: Individual kinase domains are still at the limits of current cryo-electron microscopy technology.
source: New advances in cryo-electron microscopy are continually lowering the mass limit of particles accessible for high-resolution structure determination, but individual kinase domains are still at the limits of current technology (Herzik et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Herzik et al., 2019.

claim: The formation of a crystal lattice requires contacts between the molecules that make up the unit cell and neighboring unit cells.
source: The formation of a crystal lattice requires contacts between (a) the molecules that make up the unit cell and (b) neighboring unit cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about crystallography.

claim: Crystal lattice contacts do not form accidentally, but rely on an empirical combination of solvent molecules that promote the regular packing of molecules together.
source: These contacts do not form accidentally, but rely on an empirical combination of solvent molecules that promote the regular packing of molecules together.
evidence: This is established knowledge about crystallography.

claim: The loss of entropy in crystal lattice formation is offset by a combination of enthalpic free energy gain and the gain in entropy caused by the de-solvation of protein surfaces involved in lattice contacts.
source: Since a crystal lattice is entropically unfavorable, the loss of entropy is offset by a combination of enthalpic free energy gain and the gain in entropy caused by the de-solvation of protein surfaces involved in lattice contacts (Rupp, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rupp, 2009.

claim: The underlying crystal structure represents a snapshot of an energetically favorable state under the conditions of crystallization, which has a large potential to misrepresent protein-protein contacts.
source: As such, the underlying structure represents a snapshot of an energetically favorable state under the conditions of crystallization, which has a large potential to misrepresent protein-protein contacts (Krissinel, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Krissinel, 2010.

claim: Interfaces observed in crystal lattices must be carefully validated biochemically.
source: This necessitates that interfaces observed in crystal lattices are carefully validated biochemically.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the limitations of crystallography.

claim: The trans-autophosphorylation reaction requires the exchange of activation loop segments between opposing protomers in a dimer.
source: The trans-autophosphorylation reaction requires the exchange of activation loop segments between opposing protomers in a dimer.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the structural requirements for trans-autophosphorylation.

claim: The requirement for phosphorylation dictates that activation loop segments are flexible in their unphosphorylated state.
source: By definition, the requirement for phosphorylation dictates that these segments are flexible in their unphosphorylated state and, by extension, that the surface to which they dock in their phosphorylated conformation is not occupied.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the structural properties of activation loops.

claim: The asymmetric unit of Chk2 crystals contains a single molecule which is related to a second molecule in a neighboring asymmetric unit by a twofold axis of symmetry.
source: Such packing interactions are illustrated by the structure of the kinase domain of Chk2 (Oliver et al., 2006; Figure 6A). The asymmetric unit contains a single molecule of Chk2, which is related to a second molecule in a neighboring asymmetric unit by a twofold axis of symmetry (surface representation of dimers).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oliver et al., 2006 and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The two protomers of the Chk2 dimer interact via the exchange of their activation loops that generates equivalent interactions of residues 368–394 in trans as are normally found in cis.
source: The two protomers of the dimer interact via the exchange of their activation loops (teal, red, purple-blue) that generates equivalent interactions of residues 368–394 in trans as are normally found in cis.
evidence: This describes the structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Electron density for two nitrate ions in contact with the activation loop of each Chk2 protomer was modeled in the crystal structure.
source: Electron density for two nitrate ions (red) in contact with the activation loop of each protomer was modeled in this structure, while a second magnesium ion (green) was found in a non-physiological location in the N-lobe (Figure 6B).
evidence: This describes features observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Activation loop exchanges similar to those in Chk2 have been observed in the crystal structures of many kinases.
source: Activation loop exchanges similar to those described above have been observed in the crystal structures of many kinases, wherein part of the activation loop makes equivalent interactions in trans as in cis (Lawhorn et al., 2015; Lim et al., 2020; Marcotte et al., 2017; Mayo et al., 2019; Oliver et al., 2007; Oliver et al., 2006; Pike et al., 2008; Taylor et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The relative orientation of the kinase domains in activation loop exchanged dimers is highly variable and most likely reflects a configuration amenable to lattice formation.
source: However, the relative orientation of the kinase domains in these dimers is highly variable and most likely reflects a configuration amenable to lattice formation.
evidence: This is an inference about the structural variability observed in crystal structures.

claim: Equivalent activation loop exchanges have been observed in kinases that do not undergo autophosphorylation, such as DAPK3.
source: Whilst many of these dimers have been interpreted to correspond to intermediates on the path to trans-autophosphorylation, equivalent activation loop exchanges have been observed in kinases that do not undergo autophosphorylation, such as DAPK3 (Oliver et al., 2007), for which no physiologically relevant exchange would be required.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oliver et al., 2007.

claim: The structure of a longer construct of Chk2 containing its N-terminal FHA domain depicts a dimer formed by a domain swap between the FHA domains of each protomer.
source: The structure of a longer construct of Chk2, containing its N-terminal regulatory forkhead-associated (FHA) domain (Cai et al., 2009), depicts a dimer in the asymmetric unit, formed by a domain swap between the FHA domains of each protomer (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cai et al., 2009 and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Confirmation that the Chk2 FHA domain-swapped dimer represents the trans-autophosphorylation intermediate was precluded by absent electron density for the activation loops and an ATP-binding mutation.
source: Unfortunately, confirmation that this is indeed the case was precluded by absent electron density for the activation loops of each protomer and an ATP-binding mutation introduced into the recombinant protein for crystallization.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the structural data.

claim: The structure of the Rad53 kinase domain contains a kinase-inactivating mutation that was used to facilitate crystallization.
source: The structure of the Rad53 kinase domain is equally problematic: again, a kinase-inactivating mutation was used to facilitate crystallization (Wybenga-Groot et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wybenga-Groot et al., 2014.

claim: Superimposition of one protomer from each Chk2 and Rad53 dimer shows that the r.m.s.d. over 156 Cα atoms for the kinase domains is 0.90 Å, but this balloons to 11.50 Å over equivalent Cα atoms for the second chain.
source: However, superimposition of one protomer from each dimer shows that, whilst the r.m.s.d. over 156 Cα atoms for Chk2 and Rad53 kinase domains is 0.90 Å, this balloons to 11.50 Å over equivalent Cα atoms for the second chain.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of structural data.

claim: Recent in silico modeling and biochemistry on PKD has revealed a face-to-face trans-inhibited dimer.
source: Although not yet supported by an experimentally determined structure, recent in silico modeling and biochemistry on the closely related PKD has revealed a face-to-face trans-inhibited dimer (Reinhardt et al., 2023)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reinhardt et al., 2023.

claim: Kinetic data points towards autophosphorylation in cis for AurA.
source: Finally, AurA is a rich source of conflicting data on its mechanism of autophosphorylation. While kinetic data points towards autophosphorylation in cis (Dodson et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dodson et al., 2013.

claim: AurA activation by intermolecular trans-autophosphorylation has been inferred from several crystal structures that dimerize via exchange of their activation loops.
source: AurA activation by intermolecular trans-autophosphorylation has been inferred from several crystal structures that dimerize via exchange of their activation loops (Lim et al., 2020; Zorba et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lim et al., 2020 and Zorba et al., 2014.

claim: The structure reported by Zorba et al. for AurA lacks magnesium ions in the catalytic site of both protomers and is not compatible with phosphoryl transfer.
source: However, careful inspection of the structure reveals that Asp274 is in fact the aspartate of the DFG motif, which coordinates a magnesium ion required for ATP binding. In fact, the catalytic aspartate, Asp256, is not poised for phosphoryl transfer, having been pulled out of position by the interaction of Arg255 with a phosphate ion from the crystallization solution in the center of the exchanged activation loops (Figure 6D). The structure lacks magnesium ions in the catalytic site of both protomers and is not compatible with phosphoryl transfer.
evidence: This is an analysis of the structural data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The AurA structure reported by Zorba et al. most likely represents a crystallization artifact in which the activation loop exchanged conformation is stabilized by the coordination of a phosphate ion at its center.
source: It most likely represents a crystallization artifact in which the activation loop exchanged conformation is stabilized by the coordination of the phosphate ion at its center.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of the crystal structure.

claim: AurA has been proposed to be a redox-sensitive switch, inhibited by Coenzyme A (CoA).
source: More recently, AurA has been proposed to be a redox-sensitive switch, inhibited by Coenzyme A (CoA) (Tsuchiya et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsuchiya et al., 2020.

claim: AurA has been proposed to be activated by increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) during mitosis.
source: More recently, AurA has been proposed to be a redox-sensitive switch, inhibited by Coenzyme A (CoA) (Tsuchiya et al., 2020) or activated by increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) during mitosis (Lim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lim et al., 2020.

claim: Biochemical studies have shown that oxidation inactivates AurA irrespective of activation loop autophosphorylation.
source: Biochemical studies have shown that oxidation inactivates AurA irrespective of activation loop autophosphorylation (Byrne et al., 2020; Tsuchiya et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Byrne et al., 2020 and Tsuchiya et al., 2020.

claim: A kinase that relies on the phosphorylation of its activation loop to acquire a catalytically competent conformation must somehow be able to perform this reaction without activation loop phosphorylation.
source: Simply put, a kinase that relies on the phosphorylation of its activation loop in order to acquire a catalytically competent conformation must somehow be able to perform this reaction without activation loop phosphorylation (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the paradox of activation loop autophosphorylation, shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The autophosphorylation reaction must be mechanistically distinct from the classical substrate phosphorylation reaction.
source: This apparent paradox implies that the autophosphorylation reaction must be mechanistically distinct from the classical substrate phosphorylation reaction.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the paradox described.

claim: The consensus autophosphorylation motifs of kinases often don't resemble their canonical substrate recognition motif.
source: Circumstantial evidence that the autophosphorylation reaction is mechanistically distinct comes from the consensus autophosphorylation motifs of kinases that often don't resemble their canonical substrate recognition motif (Figure 8B; Beenstock et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beenstock et al., 2016 and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A separation of function mutant of PKD in which canonical substrate recognition was disrupted had no effect on autophosphorylation in cis.
source: Experimental evidence that this is the case for at least one kinase has recently been provided by a separation of function mutant of PKD, in which canonical substrate recognition by the conserved glutamate/aspartate in the αD helix (Figure 1A and E) was disrupted (Reinhardt et al., 2023). Whilst mutation of this residue to asparagine was sufficient to completely abrogate phosphorylation of the substrate peptide in trans, it had no effect on autophosphorylation in cis (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reinhardt et al., 2023 and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Kinases are not particularly abundant molecules, with an average concentration in the low-mid nanomolar range.
source: Kinases are not particularly abundant molecules, with an average concentration in the low-mid nanomolar range (Figure 8C; Hein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hein et al., 2015 and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Eukaryotic cells have protein concentrations estimated to be in the region of 200–300 mg/ml.
source: Eukaryotic cells are large and crowded places with protein concentrations estimated to be in the region of 200–300 mg/ml (Wiśniewski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wiśniewski et al., 2014.

claim: By pure diffusion, the average protein with a half-life of 15 hr is estimated to undergo less than 0.1 interactions with another copy of itself.
source: By pure diffusion, the average protein with a half-life of 15 hr (relatively long-lived) is estimated to undergo less than 0.1 interactions with another copy of itself (Batada et al., 2004), an estimate which does not even take into account the required geometry for catalysis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Batada et al., 2004.

claim: Any bi-molecular reaction, including trans-autophosphorylation, requires the coordinated assembly of two molecules with high temporal and spatial fidelity.
source: As such, any bi-molecular reaction, including trans-autophosphorylation, requires the coordinated assembly of two molecules with high temporal and spatial fidelity.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the diffusion limitations described.

claim: Many receptor tyrosine kinases have been observed as pre-formed, inactive dimers.
source: Many receptor tyrosine kinases, for example, have been observed as pre-formed, inactive dimers. Ligand-induced conformational changes transform these receptors into a state in which they are competent of autophosphorylation (Freed et al., 2015; Maruyama, 2015; Moriki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Freed et al., 2015, Maruyama, 2015, and Moriki et al., 2001.

claim: Ligand-induced conformational changes transform pre-formed receptor tyrosine kinase dimers into a state competent for autophosphorylation.
source: Many receptor tyrosine kinases, for example, have been observed as pre-formed, inactive dimers. Ligand-induced conformational changes transform these receptors into a state in which they are competent of autophosphorylation (Freed et al., 2015; Maruyama, 2015; Moriki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Freed et al., 2015, Maruyama, 2015, and Moriki et al., 2001.

claim: Other kinases can be locally concentrated on a membrane by their specific binding to a lipid second messenger, thereby facilitating autophosphorylation.
source: Other kinases can be locally concentrated on a membrane by their specific binding to a lipid second messenger, thereby facilitating autophosphorylation (Chung et al., 2019; Levina et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2019, Levina et al., 2022, and Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Early kinetic data indicated that autophosphorylation of IRK could occur in both cis and trans.
source: Early kinetic data indicated that autophosphorylation of IRK could occur in both cis (Shoelson et al., 1991; Yamada et al., 1992) and trans (Cobbs et al., 1989; Frattali et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shoelson et al., 1991, Yamada et al., 1992, Cobbs et al., 1989, and Frattali et al., 1992.

claim: Structural and biochemical studies of IGFR1 and FGFR3 have concluded that the autophosphorylation reaction occurs in trans.
source: However, structural and biochemical studies of related kinases, including insulin-like growth factor receptor 1 (IGFR1) and fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3), have since concluded that the reaction occurs in trans (Chen et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2020 and Wu et al., 2008.

claim: IGFR1 has been trapped in a symmetric dimer in which the activation loop of both protomers is in the active site of the opposing protomer.
source: Indeed, evidence that this reaction can be performed in trans has been obtained from a number of crystal structures in which the activation loop of both protomers (Wu et al., 2008) (symmetric, Figure 8D)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2008 and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: FGFR3 has been trapped in an asymmetric dimer in which the activation loop of just one protomer is in the active site of the opposing protomer.
source: Indeed, evidence that this reaction can be performed in trans has been obtained from a number of crystal structures in which the activation loop of both protomers (Wu et al., 2008) (symmetric, Figure 8D) or just one (Chen et al., 2020) (asymmetric, Figure 8E) is trapped in the active site of the opposing protomer.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2020 and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: IGFR1 has also been trapped in an asymmetric dimer that is different from the FGFR1 asymmetric dimer, yet still positions the activation loop tyrosine for phosphoryl transfer.
source: The promiscuity of lattice contacts is further evidenced by the trapping of IGFR1 in an asymmetric dimer that is again different from the FGFR1 asymmetric dimer, yet still positions the activation loop tyrosine for phosphoryl transfer (Nemecek et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nemecek et al., 2010 and Xu et al., 2015.

claim: A two-step trans-autophosphorylation mechanism has been proposed for PAK and IRAK4 based on their crystal structures.
source: While IGFR1 might accomplish trans-autophosphorylation of each protomer simultaneously, FGFR3 would presumably need to go through a two-step reaction mechanism. Such a mechanism has also been proposed for other kinases, including p21-activated kinase (PAK) and Interleukin 1 (IL-1) receptor-associated kinase 4 (IRAK4), based on their crystal structures (Ferrao et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ferrao et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2011.

claim: The kinase domain of IRAK1 has been proposed to form heterodimers with phosphorylated, but not unphosphorylated, IRAK4, leading to a model in which IRAK4 phosphorylates IRAK1.
source: Interestingly, the kinase domain of IRAK1, which apparently does not homodimerize, has been proposed to form heterodimers with phosphorylated, but not unphosphorylated, IRAK4, leading to a model in which IRAK4 phosphorylates IRAK1 (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: The activation loop adopts the same conformation in cis, trans symmetric, trans asymmetric, and trans substrate structures, with the tyrosine poised for phosphate transfer from ATP.
source: Zooming in on the conformation of the activation loop surrounding the phosphorylated tyrosine in the cis, trans symmetric, trans asymmetric, and trans substrate structures reveals that the activation loop adopts the same conformation in each case, with the tyrosine poised for transfer of phosphate from ATP to its hydroxyl group (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8H and describes structural observations.

claim: Cis, trans symmetric, trans asymmetric, and trans substrate reactions are all stereochemically possible based on crystal structures.
source: We can, therefore, conclude from these structures that cis, trans symmetric, trans asymmetric, and trans substrate reactions are all stereochemically possible.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis.

claim: What we see in a crystal lattice and what we can observe in a test tube do not necessarily reflect reality in the cell.
source: Does that mean that they can all happen in the cell? The answer to this question is more complicated and depends on the factors that limit each of these reactions, including local concentration and the available conformational space that can be sampled. Many of these mechanisms are surely rooted in strong biochemical evidence, but, once again, we should be careful not to let our eyes deceive us: what we see in a crystal lattice and what we can observe in a test tube do not necessarily reflect reality in the cell.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of in vitro data.
